parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the model, describe the difference between α-glucose and β-glucose.

rubric.point: Describes that the –OH group on carbon 1 points below the ring in α-glucose and above the ring in β-glucose (the rest of the molecule is the same).
accept: the carbon-1 OH is down in alpha and up in beta
they differ only in the position of the hydroxyl on carbon 1

parts.sample: The two forms are identical except at carbon 1: in α-glucose the –OH on carbon 1 points below the ring, and in β-glucose it points above the ring.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain, using the model, how linking β-glucose units allows cellulose to form strong fibers.

rubric.point: Explains that β links flip every other glucose so the chain is straight; straight chains lie side by side and form many hydrogen bonds between –OH groups of neighboring chains, binding them into fibers.
accept: straight chains pack in parallel and hydrogen-bond to each other
alternating flipped units give straight chains held together by many hydrogen bonds

parts.sample: In cellulose each β link turns the next glucose upside down, so the chain runs straight instead of coiling. Straight chains lie side by side, and the –OH groups on neighboring chains form many hydrogen bonds, binding the chains into strong fibers.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Human saliva contains an enzyme that hydrolyzes starch but not cellulose, although both are made only of glucose. Explain this difference.

rubric.point: Explains that the enzyme fits the shape of the α glycosidic bond in starch; the β bond in cellulose holds the units at a different angle (shape), so the enzyme cannot bind or hydrolyze it.
accept: enzymes fit the bond shape they cut; alpha and beta bonds have different shapes
the enzyme is shaped for alpha linkages, so it does not fit beta linkages

parts.sample: The enzyme fits the shape of the α glycosidic bonds between glucose units in starch. In cellulose the bonds are β, which hold the glucose units at a different angle, so the enzyme does not fit them and cannot hydrolyze them.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Glycogen, the animal storage polysaccharide, is like the starch chain in the model but has many more branches. Explain one advantage to an animal of storing glucose in a highly branched polymer.

rubric.point: Explains that branching gives many chain ends where enzymes can remove glucose units at the same time, so glucose can be released quickly when energy is needed (also accept: a compact molecule that stores many glucose units in little space).
accept: many ends allow fast release of glucose
branches make the molecule compact, packing a lot of glucose into a small space

parts.sample: Every branch ends in a free chain end, and enzymes remove glucose from those ends. A highly branched molecule has many ends, so many glucose units can be released at once when the animal suddenly needs energy, for example in a working muscle.
